questiontext.text: In the W-method, what is the characterizing set W?

answer.text: A set of input sequences that together tell every pair of states apart — any two states differ on the output of at least one sequence in W

feedback.text: Correct — W distinguishes states by their output responses.

answer.text: One shortest input sequence that reaches each state, including ε

feedback.text: That describes the state cover P, not W.

answer.text: The state cover together with each cover sequence extended by one input

feedback.text: That is the transition cover, not W.

answer.text: The complete list of tests fed to the implementation

feedback.text: That is the whole test suite; W is only one ingredient of it.

generalfeedback.text: The characterizing (distinguishing) set W holds input sequences such that any two distinct states of the machine produce different outputs on at least one sequence in W. In the Explorer's example W = {a, aa}.

questiontext.text: What is the state cover P in the W-method?

answer.text: A set holding one shortest input sequence that reaches each state, including ε for the initial state

feedback.text: Correct — P reaches every state, ε for the start state.

answer.text: A set of sequences that distinguishes every pair of states

feedback.text: That is the characterizing set W.

answer.text: Every transition followed by a distinguishing sequence

feedback.text: That mixes ingredients; P is only about reaching states.

answer.text: The union of all input sequences up to length m

feedback.text: That is the X^≤m middle segment, not P.

generalfeedback.text: The state cover P contains, for each state, one shortest input sequence reaching it — with ε (empty sequence) covering the initial state. In the example P = {ε, a, aa}.

questiontext.text: How is the transition cover built in the W-method?

answer.text: The state cover P together with P concatenated with one more input symbol: P ∪ P·X

feedback.text: Correct — P ∪ P·X takes every transition at least once.

answer.text: The state cover P concatenated with the characterizing set W

feedback.text: That is closer to the suite; the transition cover does not append W.

answer.text: Every pair of states joined by a distinguishing sequence

feedback.text: That is not how the transition cover is defined.

answer.text: The union of all input sequences up to length m

feedback.text: That is the X^≤m segment, not the transition cover.

generalfeedback.text: The transition cover is P ∪ P·X: each state-cover sequence, and each such sequence extended by one input symbol. This forces every transition to be exercised.

questiontext.text: What does conformance testing with the W-method check?

answer.text: Whether an implementation behaves the same as the specification FSM

feedback.text: Correct — conformance means the implementation matches the spec machine.

answer.text: Whether the specification FSM is minimal

feedback.text: Minimality is a precondition of the method, not what conformance testing checks.

answer.text: Whether the implementation's source code compiles

feedback.text: Compilation is unrelated to behavioural conformance.

answer.text: Whether the implementation is fast enough

feedback.text: That is performance testing, not conformance.

generalfeedback.text: Conformance testing asks whether the black-box implementation produces the same outputs as the specification FSM on every relevant input sequence. The W-suite is a set of such input sequences.

questiontext.text: Which expression is the full W-method test suite (as shown in the Explorer)?

answer.text: (P ∪ P·X) · X^≤m · W

feedback.text: Correct — transition cover, then the middle X^≤m segment, then W.

answer.text: P · W

feedback.text: That omits both the P·X extension and the X^≤m middle segment.

answer.text: P ∪ W

feedback.text: The suite concatenates its parts; it is not a union of P and W.

answer.text: (P ∪ P·X) · X^≤m

feedback.text: That drops the characterizing set W, so landing states are never checked.

generalfeedback.text: The Explorer builds the suite as (P ∪ P·X) · X^≤m · W: the transition cover, concatenated with input sequences up to length m, concatenated with the characterizing set.

questiontext.text: The spec is a Mealy machine. Where does a Mealy machine produce its output?

answer.text: On its transitions — the output depends on the current state and the input

feedback.text: Correct — Mealy outputs are labelled on the transitions.

answer.text: In its states — the output depends only on the current state

feedback.text: That describes a Moore machine, not Mealy.

answer.text: Only when it reaches a final state

feedback.text: The machine emits an output on every transition, not only at the end.

answer.text: A Mealy machine produces no output

feedback.text: Mealy machines do emit outputs — on each transition.

generalfeedback.text: In a Mealy machine each transition carries an output that depends on both the source state and the input, e.g. q1 —a/0→ q2. (A Moore machine attaches output to states instead.)

questiontext.text: In the state cover P, the empty sequence ε is the cover entry for which state?

answer.text: The initial state q1

feedback.text: Correct — with no inputs the machine is at its start state.

answer.text: q2

feedback.text: q2 needs input a; its cover entry is a, not ε.

answer.text: q3

feedback.text: q3 needs aa; ε does not reach it.

answer.text: Every state at once

feedback.text: ε only leaves the machine at its initial state.

generalfeedback.text: Feeding no input (ε) leaves the machine in its initial state q1, so ε is q1's entry in P.

questiontext.text: In the Explorer's example, how many sequences are in the transition cover (P ∪ P·X) after removing duplicates?

questiontext.text: In the suite formula, what does the · operator mean between two sets of sequences?

answer.text: Concatenation — each sequence from the left set followed by each sequence from the right set

feedback.text: Correct — it is set concatenation of sequences.

answer.text: Set union of the two sets

feedback.text: Union is written ∪; · is concatenation.

answer.text: Set intersection

feedback.text: · is not intersection; it joins sequences end to end.

answer.text: The Cartesian product of the two state sets

feedback.text: The operator works on sequences, producing concatenations, not state pairs.

generalfeedback.text: A·B is the set of all concatenations x·y where x comes from A and y from B — for example {a}·{a, aa} = {aa, aaa}.

questiontext.text: In the specification FSM, input a in state q1 emits output 0 and moves to state q2.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the transition is q1 —a/0→ q2.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The table shows q1 —a/0→ q2, so the statement is true.

generalfeedback.text: The specification defines q1 —a/0→ q2: on input a from q1 the machine outputs 0 and transitions to q2.

questiontext.text: What is the shortest input sequence that reaches state q3 from the initial state?

answer.text: aa

feedback.text: Correct — q1 —a→ q2 —a→ q3.

answer.text: a

feedback.text: a only reaches q2.

answer.text: ab

feedback.text: q1 —a→ q2 —b→ q1 returns to q1, not q3.

answer.text: b

feedback.text: q1 —b→ q1 is a self-loop; it never leaves q1.

generalfeedback.text: From q1, input a moves to q2, and a second a moves to q3, so aa is the shortest reaching sequence — this is q3's entry in the state cover P.

questiontext.text: What is the shortest input sequence that distinguishes q2 from q3?

answer.text: a — q2 outputs 1, q3 outputs 0

feedback.text: Correct — one input a already separates them.

answer.text: b — both output 1

feedback.text: q2 —b/1→ and q3 —b/1→ emit the same output, so b does not distinguish them.

answer.text: aa

feedback.text: a alone already distinguishes q2 and q3; aa is longer than needed.

answer.text: ab

feedback.text: The shortest distinguishing sequence is a, not ab.

generalfeedback.text: q2 —a/1→ q3 emits 1, but q3 —a/0→ q3 emits 0; the outputs differ on the very first input, so a distinguishes q2 and q3.

questiontext.text: Why is a sequence from W appended to every prefix in the suite?

answer.text: It turns the state reached by the prefix into an observable output trace, so a wrong landing state shows up as wrong output

feedback.text: Correct — W makes the internal state observable through output.

answer.text: It makes each prefix reach a new, previously unvisited state

feedback.text: W checks the state reached; it does not reach new states.

answer.text: It shortens the suite by removing duplicate prefixes

feedback.text: Appending W does not deduplicate; it verifies states.

answer.text: It guards each transition with a boolean condition

feedback.text: Guards belong to the FSM, not to the suite construction.

generalfeedback.text: A black-box tester cannot read internal states directly. By appending a distinguishing sequence from W, the state reached by a prefix is exposed as a specific output trace, so a next-state fault becomes a visible output difference.

questiontext.text: Which sequence belongs to the transition cover (P ∪ P·X) but not to P itself?

answer.text: ab

feedback.text: Correct — ab is a (in P) extended by b, so it is in P·X but not P.

answer.text: aa

feedback.text: aa is already in P (it reaches q3).

answer.text: ε

feedback.text: ε is in P (it covers q1).

answer.text: a

feedback.text: a is in P (it reaches q2).

generalfeedback.text: P = {ε, a, aa}. Extending each by one input gives P·X, which contributes new sequences like b, ab, aaa, aab. So ab is in the transition cover but not in P.

questiontext.text: With |P| = 3 and |X| = 2, how many sequences are in P ∪ P·X after removing duplicates for this FSM?

feedback.text: Correct — 3 from P plus 6 from P·X, minus the 2 duplicates a and aa.
9 is 3 + 6 before removing the duplicates a and aa.
6 is the size of P·X alone.
Only two sequences (a and aa) are duplicated, giving 9 − 2 = 7.

generalfeedback.text: P·X = {a, b, aa, ab, aaa, aab}. Union with P = {ε, a, aa} removes the duplicates a and aa, leaving {ε, a, aa, b, ab, aaa, aab} — 7 sequences.

questiontext.text: Match the ingredient to its role: in the W-method, the characterizing set W serves to…

answer.text: distinguish states by their output responses, so the state reached can be verified

feedback.text: Correct — that is exactly W's job.

answer.text: reach every state at least once

feedback.text: That is the role of the state cover P.

answer.text: take every transition at least once

feedback.text: That is the role of the transition cover P ∪ P·X.

answer.text: enumerate all input sequences up to length m

feedback.text: That is the role of the X^≤m middle segment.

generalfeedback.text: Each ingredient has a distinct role: P reaches states, P ∪ P·X takes transitions, X^≤m allows for extra states, and W distinguishes states so the reached state is verifiable.

name.text: Divergence position for q1 vs q2

answer.text: Position 1 — q1 outputs 0, q2 outputs 1

answer.text: They never differ

questiontext.text: When m = 0, what is the middle segment X^≤m of the suite?

answer.text: {ε} — so the suite reduces to (P ∪ P·X) · W

feedback.text: Correct — X^≤0 is just the empty sequence.

answer.text: {a, b}

answer.text: {ε, a, b}

questiontext.text: Running the input sequence aa from state q1, what output does the Mealy machine emit?

feedback.text: Correct — q1 —a/0→ q2 —a/1→ q3 emits 0 then 1.
00 is what q3 emits on aa, not q1.
The first a from q1 emits 0, not 1.
The outputs are 0 then 1, giving 01, not 10.

generalfeedback.text: From q1: a gives output 0 and moves to q2; the next a gives output 1 and moves to q3. So the trace is 01.

name.text: Why aa is needed in W

questiontext.text: Why does W include aa rather than rely on a alone?

answer.text: Input a gives output 0 from both q1 and q3, so a cannot separate them; aa does (01 vs 00)

feedback.text: Correct — aa is needed to tell q1 and q3 apart.

answer.text: a is not a valid input, so a longer sequence is required

feedback.text: a is a valid input; the issue is that it fails to separate q1 and q3.

answer.text: aa is shorter and therefore preferred

feedback.text: aa is longer than a; it is included because it is necessary, not shorter.

answer.text: W must contain every sequence of length 2

feedback.text: W contains only what is needed to distinguish states, not all length-2 sequences.

generalfeedback.text: q1 —a/0→ and q3 —a/0→ both emit 0, so a alone cannot separate q1 from q3. Extending to aa gives 01 from q1 versus 00 from q3, which distinguishes them — so W must include aa.

questiontext.text: How is each test sequence in the W-suite structured?

answer.text: A transition-cover prefix, then a middle segment from X^≤m, then a distinguishing suffix from W

feedback.text: Correct — prefix · middle · W-suffix.

answer.text: A W-suffix, then a transition-cover prefix

feedback.text: The order is prefix first, then W last, not the reverse.

answer.text: Only a sequence from W

feedback.text: Each test also carries a cover prefix and a middle segment.

answer.text: Only a sequence from the state cover P

feedback.text: A W-suite test also appends the middle segment and a W suffix.

generalfeedback.text: Each suite element is (cover sequence) · (middle sequence from X^≤m) · (distinguishing sequence from W): reach or exercise a transition, optionally wander through extra inputs, then verify the resulting state.

questiontext.text: Which ingredient of the W-method forces every transition to be taken at least once?

answer.text: The transition cover, P ∪ P·X

feedback.text: Correct — extending P by one input takes each outgoing transition.

answer.text: The characterizing set W

feedback.text: W distinguishes states; it does not by itself take every transition.

answer.text: The X^≤m middle segment

feedback.text: X^≤m allows for extra states; it is not what guarantees transition coverage.

answer.text: The state cover P alone

feedback.text: P only reaches states; the P·X extension is needed to take every transition.

generalfeedback.text: P reaches each state, and appending one further input (P·X) takes each outgoing transition. Together, P ∪ P·X exercises every transition of the spec.

name.text: Size of W in the example

answer.text: 2 — namely a and aa

feedback.text: Correct — W = {a, aa}.
One sequence is not enough: a cannot distinguish q1 from q3, so aa is also needed.
The Explorer's W has exactly two sequences.
6 is the number of transitions, not the size of W.

generalfeedback.text: W = {a, aa} — two sequences: a separates q1/q2 and q2/q3, and aa separates q1/q3.

questiontext.text: What is the shortest input sequence that distinguishes q1 from q3?

answer.text: aa — q1 gives 01, q3 gives 00

feedback.text: Correct — the outputs differ at the second position.

answer.text: a — both give 0

feedback.text: q1 —a/0→ and q3 —a/0→ both emit 0, so a does not distinguish them.

answer.text: b — both give 1

questiontext.text: With m = 0, how many distinct tests does the Explorer's suite contain for this FSM?

feedback.text: Correct — the Explorer reports 11 distinct tests at m = 0.
14 is 7 × 2 before removing duplicate sequences.
The deduplicated suite has 11 tests, not 9.
23 is the suite size at m = 1, not m = 0.

questiontext.text: The Explorer's mutant rewires q3 —b→ from q2 to q1 while keeping the output 1. What kind of fault is this?

answer.text: A transfer (next-state) fault — correct output, wrong target state

feedback.text: Correct — the output is unchanged but the destination is wrong.

answer.text: An output fault — the transition emits the wrong symbol

feedback.text: The output stays 1; only the target state changed, so it is not an output fault.

answer.text: An extra-state fault — the implementation added a state

feedback.text: No state was added; an existing transition was redirected.

answer.text: A sneak path — an event accepted where none was specified

feedback.text: The event b was already specified in q3; only its target moved.

generalfeedback.text: The mutant keeps q3 —b/1→ but sends it to q1 instead of q2: same output, wrong next state. That is a classic transfer (next-state) fault — the case transition coverage alone can miss.

questiontext.text: Why can plain transition coverage miss this mutant while the W-suite catches it?

answer.text: Transition coverage only checks that the transition fires with the right output; it does not verify which state you land in. Appending W checks the landing state

feedback.text: Correct — W exposes the wrong target that coverage ignores.

answer.text: Transition coverage never exercises the q3 —b→ transition at all

feedback.text: It does exercise it; it just cannot see the wrong target without W.

answer.text: The mutant changes the output, which coverage cannot observe

feedback.text: The output is unchanged; the target state is what differs.

answer.text: Transition coverage requires a longer alphabet

feedback.text: Alphabet size is not the issue; verifying the reached state is.

generalfeedback.text: Taking the transition with matching output satisfies transition coverage even though it ends in the wrong state. The W-suite appends a distinguishing sequence after the transition, so the wrong landing state produces a different output trace and the fault is caught.

questiontext.text: In the Explorer at m = 0, the first suite test that exposes the mutant is aaba. How do spec and mutant differ on it?

answer.text: The spec outputs 0111 but the mutant outputs 0110 — they diverge at the last symbol

feedback.text: Correct — the wrong target state changes the final output.

answer.text: The spec outputs 0110 and the mutant outputs 0111

feedback.text: It is the other way round: spec 0111, mutant 0110.

answer.text: They produce the same output but the mutant is shorter

feedback.text: Both traces have the same length; the outputs differ.

answer.text: Both output 0111, so the test passes

feedback.text: The mutant outputs 0110, so the test fails.

generalfeedback.text: On aaba the spec runs q1→q2→q3→q2→q3 emitting 0111, while the mutant's q3 —b→ q1 makes it run q1→q2→q3→q1→q2 emitting 0110 — the last output differs, exposing the fault.

questiontext.text: The W-method's fault-detection guarantee holds under which assumption about the implementation?

answer.text: The implementation has at most m extra states beyond the n states of the spec

feedback.text: Correct — the guarantee is relative to a bound of m extra states.

answer.text: The implementation has exactly the same states with the same names

feedback.text: The method allows extra states (up to m); identical naming is not required.

answer.text: The implementation uses a binary input alphabet

feedback.text: Alphabet size is unrelated to the guarantee.

answer.text: The specification contains no self-loops

feedback.text: Self-loops are allowed; the assumption is about extra states.

generalfeedback.text: The W-method guarantees detection of output and transfer faults only if the implementation has at most m extra states beyond the spec's n states — the middle segment X^≤m is what covers those extra states.

questiontext.text: What happens to the guarantee if the implementation has more extra states than the assumed bound m?

answer.text: The guarantee is lost — some faults can escape the suite undetected

feedback.text: Correct — beyond m extra states the completeness proof no longer holds.

answer.text: Nothing changes; the guarantee still holds for any implementation

feedback.text: The guarantee is conditional on the extra-state bound.

answer.text: The suite becomes infinite

feedback.text: The suite stays finite; only the guarantee weakens.

answer.text: W stops being able to distinguish the spec's states

feedback.text: W still distinguishes the spec's states; it just may not reach a hidden extra state.

generalfeedback.text: The X^≤m segment only accounts for up to m extra states. If the implementation hides more, a faulty state can be reached only by sequences longer than the suite exercises, so the fault may go undetected.

name.text: What drives suite growth with m

questiontext.text: In the Explorer the suite grows 11 → 23 → 47 as m goes 0 → 1 → 2. What drives this growth?

answer.text: Each increment of m adds longer middle sequences (X^≤m grows by a power of |X|), multiplying the number of tests

feedback.text: Correct — the X^≤m middle is what expands with m.

answer.text: W grows with m, adding more distinguishing sequences

feedback.text: W depends on the spec, not on m; it stays {a, aa}.

answer.text: The state cover P grows with m

feedback.text: P depends on the spec's states, not on m.

answer.text: The input alphabet grows with m

feedback.text: The alphabet is fixed at {a, b}.

generalfeedback.text: Only the middle segment X^≤m depends on m. As m increases it includes longer input sequences (a |X|-power more each step), so the suite roughly multiplies by the alphabet size — 11, 23, 47 in the example.

name.text: Why W verifies the exact state

questiontext.text: Why does appending W let the suite verify the exact state reached, not just the outputs seen along the way?

answer.text: Any two distinct states of a minimal FSM differ on some sequence in W, so a wrong landing state yields a different W-output trace

feedback.text: Correct — W is a complete separator of states.

answer.text: W resets the machine to its initial state before checking

feedback.text: W does not reset the machine; it reads the current state's behaviour.

answer.text: W lists every reachable state by name

feedback.text: W is a set of input sequences, not a list of state names.

answer.text: W is applied only to the initial state

feedback.text: W is appended after each prefix, i.e. to whatever state the prefix reaches.

generalfeedback.text: Because W distinguishes every pair of states, two different landing states must disagree on at least one W sequence. So if a prefix lands in the wrong state, the appended W produces a different, observable output trace.

questiontext.text: Under its assumption, the W-method is guaranteed to detect which classes of fault?

answer.text: Output faults and transfer (next-state) faults

feedback.text: Correct — both are guaranteed under the extra-state bound.

answer.text: Only output faults

feedback.text: Transfer faults are also caught, as the mutant example shows.

answer.text: Only missing states

feedback.text: The method targets output and transfer faults, not just missing states.

answer.text: Timing and performance faults

feedback.text: The W-method is about functional behaviour, not timing.

generalfeedback.text: Given at most m extra states, the W-suite detects every output fault (wrong symbol) and every transfer fault (wrong next state) — the transition cover exercises each transition and W verifies both its output and its resulting state.

name.text: Why the spec must be minimal

questiontext.text: Why must the specification FSM be minimal (no two equivalent states) for the W-method to work as intended?

answer.text: Only then does W distinguish all n states, and n is the true state count against which the extra-state bound is measured

feedback.text: Correct — minimality makes W a complete separator and fixes n.

answer.text: Minimality makes the suite smaller

feedback.text: Suite size is a side effect; the real reason is correctness of W and n.

answer.text: Minimality is only a diagram-drawing convention

feedback.text: It is a correctness requirement, not a drawing choice.

answer.text: Minimality lets ε be dropped from the state cover

feedback.text: ε always covers the initial state; minimality does not remove it.

generalfeedback.text: If the spec had equivalent states, no W sequence could tell them apart and the count n would overstate the distinct behaviours. Minimality guarantees W separates all n states and that n is the correct baseline for the at-most-m-extra-states assumption.

name.text: How suite size scales with n

questiontext.text: For a fixed alphabet and m, how does the W-suite size scale with the number of states n?

answer.text: Polynomially — roughly n² (state cover × characterizing set) times |X|^(m+1)

feedback.text: Correct — |P| and |W| each scale with n, giving a polynomial, not exponential, size.

answer.text: It does not grow with n — the characterizing set has constant size

feedback.text: |W| grows with n, so the suite is not constant in n.

answer.text: Linearly in n — exactly one test per state

feedback.text: Both |P| and |W| scale with n, so the product is more than linear.

answer.text: Exponentially in n — one dedicated test per pair of states

feedback.text: The growth is polynomial (about n²), not exponential in n.

generalfeedback.text: The transition cover scales with n and W scales with n, so their product is about n²; the X^≤m middle adds a |X|^(m+1) factor. Overall the suite grows polynomially in n for fixed alphabet and m.

name.text: Why the same-output mutant is hard

questiontext.text: The mutant keeps the same output (1) on the rewired transition. Why does that make it hard to catch?

answer.text: Any test that only reads the output of that one transition passes; the error surfaces only later, through W-driven behaviour from the wrong state

feedback.text: Correct — the fault is only visible downstream, via W.

answer.text: The transition can never be reached by any test

feedback.text: It is reachable; the difficulty is that its immediate output looks correct.

answer.text: The mutant produces no output at all

feedback.text: It still outputs 1; the output is simply unchanged.

answer.text: The fault changes the input alphabet

feedback.text: The alphabet is unchanged; only the target state moved.

generalfeedback.text: Because the transition's own output is unchanged, checks that stop at that transition see nothing wrong. The wrong target state only shows up when a distinguishing sequence from W is run afterward, revealing the different downstream behaviour.

questiontext.text: At m = 0 the Explorer reports that 2 of 11 suite tests catch the mutant. What is the practical significance of that count?

answer.text: Only one failing test is needed to expose the fault; the suite guarantees at least one exists under the assumption

feedback.text: Correct — completeness needs just one witness, and here there are two.

answer.text: The mutant is caught only 2/11 of the time, at random

feedback.text: The suite is deterministic; those two tests always fail on the mutant.

answer.text: You must run all 11 tests before the fault can be seen

feedback.text: Either of the two failing tests alone already exposes it.

answer.text: 2 out of 11 means the suite is incomplete

feedback.text: Completeness only requires at least one failing test; the suite is complete under the assumption.

generalfeedback.text: A fault is exposed as soon as one test fails. That 2 of 11 tests catch the mutant simply means the guarantee (at least one failing test under the extra-state assumption) is comfortably met.

name.text: How transition cover and W combine

questiontext.text: How do the transition cover and W work together in the suite?

answer.text: The transition cover drives the machine through every transition; W then checks that each transition ended in the correct state and produced the correct output

feedback.text: Correct — cover for reachability, W for state verification.

answer.text: W chooses which transitions to exercise, and the cover verifies the outputs

feedback.text: Their roles are reversed: the cover exercises transitions, W verifies states.

answer.text: Both do the same job, so one is redundant

feedback.text: They play complementary roles; neither is redundant.

answer.text: The cover replaces the need for W when m = 0

feedback.text: W is appended even at m = 0; without it landing states are unverified.

generalfeedback.text: The transition cover (P ∪ P·X) guarantees every transition is taken; appending W to each such prefix turns the reached state into an observable trace, so both the output and the resulting state of every transition are checked.

name.text: Effect of choosing a larger m

questiontext.text: What is the effect of choosing a larger m in practice?

answer.text: It tolerates more possible extra states (a stronger guarantee) but enlarges the suite by a power of the alphabet, costing more tests

feedback.text: Correct — stronger guarantee, larger suite.

answer.text: It shrinks the suite while keeping the same guarantee

feedback.text: Larger m enlarges the suite, not shrinks it.

answer.text: It has no effect on the fault-detection guarantee

feedback.text: Larger m covers more extra states, strengthening the guarantee.

answer.text: It removes the extra-state assumption entirely

feedback.text: The assumption remains; m is precisely the bound in it.

generalfeedback.text: Larger m means the X^≤m segment includes longer sequences, so the suite can uncover faults hidden behind more extra states — but the number of tests grows by a factor of the alphabet size per step (11, 23, 47 in the example). It is a coverage-versus-cost trade-off.

questiontext.text: Beyond the state cover P, why does the suite also include P·X (each cover sequence extended by one input)?

answer.text: P alone only reaches states; P·X takes each outgoing transition once, so combined with W every transition's target is verified

feedback.text: Correct — P·X supplies transition coverage.

answer.text: P·X reaches states that are otherwise unreachable

feedback.text: P already reaches all states; P·X exercises the transitions between them.

answer.text: P·X replaces the need for W

feedback.text: W is still needed to verify the state each transition reaches.

answer.text: P·X is only needed for non-minimal machines

feedback.text: P·X is part of the standard construction for any spec, minimal or not.

generalfeedback.text: P reaches every state but does not necessarily take every transition. Extending each cover sequence by one input (P·X) fires each outgoing transition; appending W then confirms it landed in the right state — that is how transfer faults are caught.
